title: Quality of Bladder Cancer Information on YouTube
screen_reason: Content analysis of the first 150 YouTube videos returned for 'bladder cancer'. Videos were scored for misinformation on a five-point Likert scale by urologists/urology trainees; 44/150 (29%) had any misinformation and 31/150 (21%) a moderate-to-high amount - quantitative falsity shares with an explicit denominator. DISCERN quality shares are also reported (QUALITY rows).

estimates.notes: The Results sentence with the counts reads 'Forty-four videos had any misinformation (score >1 out of 5), and these videos had 1 483 859 views, while 21% had a moderate to high amount of misinformation (score >2 out of 5) and reached 1 289 314 viewers.' - the two-column text rendering interleaves it with the adjacent table, so the contiguous verbatim span quoted in source_quote is the Discussion's 'misinformation in 29% of the top bladder cancer videos' (from 'Our finding of misinformation in 29% of the top bladder cancer videos on YouTube is in line with previous studies'). Broad (any misinformation) variant; the stricter moderate-to-high variant is a separate row. Value is the exact part/whole share of the verbatim count 44 over the verbatim denominator 150 (Table 1's misinformation-score distribution corroborates: 106 scored 1, so 44 scored >1); the paper's own rounded statement is 29%. Search date not reported, so year = publication year 2020.

Separate, most-viewed sample (not a definition variant of the 150-video rows but a different denominator - a view-ranked set). Flagged borderline/medium confidence because neither 28% nor 78% is an integer share of 20 (28% of 20 = 5.6; 78% of 20 = 15.6); the percentages are consistent with n=18 (5/18 = 27.8%, 14/18 = 77.8%), so the effective denominator may be smaller than 20. Supplementary Table 4 is not in the text file, so the counts cannot be verified. An adjudicator may prefer to drop this row for that reason.

missed_or_uncertain: Not extracted: commercial bias 26/150 (17%), complementary/alternative medicine 24/150 (16%), favours new technology 28/150 (19%) - bias/promotion codes, not veracity judgements; 'moderate to poor in 78%' among the 20 most-viewed videos (same non-integer denominator problem as the 28% row, and it is a QUALITY duplicate); comment-section behaviours (medical advice requested 20%, given 9%, social support 19%, behaviour change 12%, advertising <1%); PEMAT medians (33% actionability, 71% understandability - scale scores, not shares); video reach figures (1,483,859 views for any-misinformation videos; 1,289,314 for high-misinformation videos; 1,848,218 for moderate-to-poor-quality videos). Those reach counts are audience counts, not shares of exposure, and no total view denominator for the 150 videos is given (Table 2's 'Total unique videos and views 119 (79) 1 918 800' is the union of the five content categories, not the corpus total), so no EXPOSURE row is derivable. The 40% (prostate cancer) and 35% (colonoscopy) misinformation figures in the discussion are cited from other papers and excluded by R8.

rob.design: Cross-sectional YouTube content analysis (Brief Correspondence). Frame: the first 150 of 242,000 videos returned for 'bladder cancer' - a rank-truncated convenience sample; search date, login status, geography and sort order are not reported. Instruments: validated PEMAT and DISCERN, plus an author-devised five-point Likert misinformation scale carried over from the authors' prostate cancer/colonoscopy studies and not defined in the text. Coding by urologists and urology trainees, independently, with 'random coding checks to verify intercoder reliability' but no reported kappa or agreement statistic. Pearson correlations relate views per month to misinformation. A supplementary re-analysis of the 20 most-viewed videos is reported but its counts are not recoverable from the text.
